items.readable_text:
Content:
When performing certain types of statistical tests (e.g., hypothesis testing), we often need to use standard cumulative distribution function (CDF) tables to carry out the test.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct CDF tables for the binomial distribution and use them to calculate probabilities.

Content:
First, recall that the probability mass function of the binomial distribution [MATH: B(n,p)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) = \binom{n}{x} \, p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots, n]

Content:
where [MATH: n] is the number of trials, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success.

Content:
Also, recall that the CDF of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is a function [MATH: F(x)] such that

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

Content:
With that in mind, let's compute the value of [MATH: F(x)] for the distribution [MATH: B(5,0.37)] at [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=1.]

Content:
To do that, we use the definition of the cumulative distribution function:

Content:
[MATH: F(0)|= P(X ≤ 0); = P(X = 0); = ((5)/(0))(0.37)^{0}(1 − 0.37)^{5 − 0}; = 1 ⋅ (0.37)^{0} ⋅ (0.63)^{5}; ≈ 0.0992; F(1)|= P(X ≤ 1); = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1); = ((5)/(0))(0.37)^{0}(1 − 0.37)^{5 − 0} + ((5)/(1))(0.37)^{1}(1 − 0.37)^{5 − 1}; = 1 ⋅ (0.37)^{0} ⋅ (0.63)^{5} + 5 ⋅ (0.37)^{1} ⋅ (0.63)^{4}; ≈ 0.3907.]

Content:
The CDF data is usually presented as a table. If we were to continue this process and calculate [MATH: F(2), F(3), F(4),] and [MATH: F(5),] our table would look as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: \quad x \quad] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] |
| [MATH: P(X\leq x)] | [MATH: \,\bbox[gainsboro, 3pt]{\color{blue}0.0992}\,] | [MATH: \,\bbox[gainsboro, 3pt]{\color{blue}0.3907}\,] | [MATH: \,0.7330\,] | [MATH: \,0.9340\,] | [MATH: \,0.9931\,] | [MATH: \,1.0000\,] |

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: F(x)] is an increasing function.
- Since [MATH: n] is the largest possible value of the binomial distribution, we have [MATH: F(n) = 1.]

sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is a function [MATH: F(x)] such that [MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

The probability mass function for the Binomial distribution [MATH: B(n,p)] is given by [MATH: f(x) = \displaystyle \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots,n.]

In our case, [MATH: n=7] and [MATH: p=0.63.]

Therefore, we compute the missing elements of the table as follows:

  • For [MATH: F(6),] we have

[MATH: F(6)|= P(X ≤ 6); = P(X ≤ 5) + P(X = 6); = F(5) + P(X = 6); = 0.7987 + ((7)/(6))(0.63)^{6}(1 − 0.63)^{7 − 6}; = 0.7987 + 7 ⋅ (0.63)^{6} ⋅ (0.37)^{1}; ≈ 0.9606.]

  • Since [MATH: n=7,] we have that [MATH: F(7) = P(X\leq 7) = 1.]

Therefore, our completed table looks as follows:

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When performing certain types of statistical tests (e.g., hypothesis testing), we often need to use standard cumulative distribution function (CDF) tables to carry out the test.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct CDF tables for the binomial distribution and use them to calculate probabilities.

Content:
First, recall that the probability mass function of the binomial distribution [MATH: B(n,p)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) = \binom{n}{x} \, p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots, n]

Content:
where [MATH: n] is the number of trials, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success.

Content:
Also, recall that the CDF of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is a function [MATH: F(x)] such that

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

Content:
With that in mind, let's compute the value of [MATH: F(x)] for the distribution [MATH: B(5,0.37)] at [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=1.]

Content:
To do that, we use the definition of the cumulative distribution function:

Content:
[MATH: F(0)|= P(X ≤ 0); = P(X = 0); = ((5)/(0))(0.37)^{0}(1 − 0.37)^{5 − 0}; = 1 ⋅ (0.37)^{0} ⋅ (0.63)^{5}; ≈ 0.0992; F(1)|= P(X ≤ 1); = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1); = ((5)/(0))(0.37)^{0}(1 − 0.37)^{5 − 0} + ((5)/(1))(0.37)^{1}(1 − 0.37)^{5 − 1}; = 1 ⋅ (0.37)^{0} ⋅ (0.63)^{5} + 5 ⋅ (0.37)^{1} ⋅ (0.63)^{4}; ≈ 0.3907.]

Content:
The CDF data is usually presented as a table. If we were to continue this process and calculate [MATH: F(2), F(3), F(4),] and [MATH: F(5),] our table would look as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: \quad x \quad] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] |
| [MATH: P(X\leq x)] | [MATH: \,\bbox[gainsboro, 3pt]{\color{blue}0.0992}\,] | [MATH: \,\bbox[gainsboro, 3pt]{\color{blue}0.3907}\,] | [MATH: \,0.7330\,] | [MATH: \,0.9340\,] | [MATH: \,0.9931\,] | [MATH: \,1.0000\,] |

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: F(x)] is an increasing function.
- Since [MATH: n] is the largest possible value of the binomial distribution, we have [MATH: F(n) = 1.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing a Binomial CDF Table

Example Prompt:
Consider the binomial random variable [MATH: X\sim B(7, 0.63).] Rounding to [MATH: 4] decimal places, fill in the missing values in the cumulative distribution function table below.

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 7] |
| [MATH: P(X \leq x)] | [MATH: 0.0009] | [MATH: 0.0123] | [MATH: 0.0701] | [MATH: 0.2341] | [MATH: 0.5134] | [MATH: 0.7987] | | |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is a function [MATH: F(x)] such that
[MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

The probability mass function for the Binomial distribution [MATH: B(n,p)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) = \displaystyle \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots,n.]

In our case, [MATH: n=7] and [MATH: p=0.63.]

Therefore, we compute the missing elements of the table as follows:

- For [MATH: F(6),] we have

[MATH: F(6)|= P(X ≤ 6); = P(X ≤ 5) + P(X = 6); = F(5) + P(X = 6); = 0.7987 + ((7)/(6))(0.63)^{6}(1 − 0.63)^{7 − 6}; = 0.7987 + 7 ⋅ (0.63)^{6} ⋅ (0.37)^{1}; ≈ 0.9606.]

- Since [MATH: n=7,] we have that [MATH: F(7) = P(X\leq 7) = 1.]

Therefore, our completed table looks as follows:

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 7] |
| [MATH: P(X \leq x)] | [MATH: 0.0009] | [MATH: 0.0123] | [MATH: 0.0701] | [MATH: 0.2341] | [MATH: 0.5134] | [MATH: 0.7987] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.9606}] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}] |
